question:
Zomato on-campus Machine Learning Engineer interview (Aug 2025, Glassdoor report). Two related questions:

- What is the difference between using **positional embeddings from a patch-CNN (trainable)** and the **non-parametric** ones used in the original "Attention Is All You Need" paper?
- Questions around **optimising voice-to-text (speech recognition) and TTS models**, and the **effect of model quantization on inference quality**.
lookingFor: Why Transformers need positional information at all
Trade-offs between learned and fixed encodings (extrapolation, flexibility, parameters)
Practical inference optimisation knowledge for speech models
Understanding what quantization does and how to measure its quality impact
answer:
**Why positions are needed.** Self-attention is permutation-equivariant: without positional information, the model sees a bag of tokens. So position is injected, usually by adding a vector to the input embedding.

**Sinusoidal (non-parametric).** Each dimension is a sine or cosine of the position at a different frequency. No parameters, so nothing to train. It is defined for any position and can in principle extrapolate to sequences longer than those seen in training (in practice extrapolation is limited), and relative offsets are expressible as a linear function of the encodings. The paper reported learned embeddings gave nearly the same quality.

**Learned (trainable), such as patch-CNN features or a learned table.** Position is a parameter the model optimises, so it can adapt to the data and modality. In vision, a CNN over patches (or a convolutional position encoding) also injects local spatial structure and works on 2D layouts. Downsides: a fixed-size table cannot handle positions beyond the trained length without interpolation (as done when ViT resolution changes), extra parameters, and more risk of overfitting on small data. Many modern models use relative or rotary encodings (RoPE, ALiBi) for better length handling.

**Optimising speech-to-text and TTS (examples).**
- Use smaller or distilled models, or streaming architectures to cut latency.
- Batch requests and use GPU-friendly kernels and caching of encoder states; export to an optimised runtime such as ONNX or TensorRT.
- Reduce audio features (sample rate, mel bins) where quality allows; use voice activity detection to skip silence.
- For TTS, the vocoder is usually the bottleneck, so choose a fast one.

**Quantization.** Store weights (and optionally activations) in lower precision such as FP16, INT8 or INT4, giving smaller models, less memory bandwidth and faster inference. The risk is accuracy loss: for ASR, a higher word error rate, especially on accents and noisy audio; for TTS, artefacts or a less natural voice. Post-training quantization is quick; quantization-aware training or per-channel scaling and keeping sensitive layers in higher precision reduce degradation. Always evaluate on a held-out set (WER for ASR, MOS or listening tests for TTS) before and after.
followUps: How do rotary embeddings (RoPE) differ from sinusoidal and learned embeddings?
How do you handle a Vision Transformer when test images have a different resolution from training?
What is the difference between post-training quantization and quantization-aware training?
How would you evaluate whether a quantized TTS model is acceptable?
